Tally, Zoho, Vyapar, custom in-house systems, via config-driven mappings
Continuous reconciliation against source ERP balances, silent-failure detection

sections.label: The Problem
sections.title: Every system told a different story about the same stock.

paragraphs.text: Every Closphere customer was a manufacturer, and every one ran on messy, partly unstructured data: ERP exports, spreadsheets, and paper challans we had to OCR. Units of measure, batches, and locations meant different things in different systems. When the numbers can't be trusted, teams go back to calling the warehouse, and the software becomes a report nobody reads.

Discovery with 50+ customers showed the same core entities everywhere: item master, units of measure, multi-location stock, batch and lot data, transaction types. The systems differed in how they expressed those entities, not in what the entities were.

sections.label: The Decision
sections.title: Build the model first. Make every connector configuration.

paragraphs.text: I invested in a canonical data model before building integrations. Connectors for Tally, Zoho, Vyapar, and custom in-house systems became mappings into that model, and the mappings became configuration-driven.

sections.label: Trust Architecture
sections.title: A silent failure is worse than a loud one.

paragraphs.text: Capability was never the hard part. Trust was. A local sync agent fed cloud aggregation, and we continuously reconciled against the source ERP's own balances. We also built detection for the scariest failure mode: sync that stops without anyone noticing.
There was no wrong customer. Every one of them improved the product. But some demanded heavy customization, and that pulled against the configuration-driven thesis the whole company was built on.

We turned part of that tension into pricing, with usage-based upselling tied to customization needs. But once, a major customer's request pushed us past capacity. I hired immediately, pulled all-nighters alongside the team to deliver, and then gave everyone a week off to reset. Since then I check team bandwidth before I commit to an ambitious ask, not after.

sections.label: Growth
sections.title: Customers sold it for us.

paragraphs.text: Referral drove about 30% of new business. We tracked activation through newsletters and word of mouth.

sections.label: Outcomes
sections.title: From 75% to 95% inventory accuracy, and a technology/IP sale.

paragraphs.text: 63 paying customers across 112 locations and 1K+ users. Inventory record accuracy went from 75% to 95%, stockouts dropped 32%, and reconciliation effort fell by more than 70%. Onboarding went from 6+ weeks to under 7 days. The company ended in a technology/IP sale.

sections.label: What I Learned
sections.title: The product was the data model.

paragraphs.text: Connectors, dashboards, and alerts were all downstream of getting the model right once. And the constraint I underestimated wasn't technical. It was my team's bandwidth.
